clue.text: Top church job for boys keeping good company with 3

indicators.note: keeping means holding something inside, so the boys enclose the next piece

parts.note: Archies are boys going by the name Archie, used here as a stand-in for boys generally
PI, short for pious, is the crossword's usual word for good
3 refers to the answer at 3-down, a crown, and the crown of the head is the pate

explanation.surface: A senior clerical post goes to some lads who mix with royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference to 3 is not to a crown worn by a king but the crown of the head, PATE.
explanation.definitionFit: The office of an archbishop is the highest post in a church's hierarchy.

clue.text: Classical runner first seen in US city

indicators.note: in means the first letter is placed inside the name of the city

parts.note: Atlanta is the capital of the US state of Georgia
A is the first letter, as in A1 or grade A

explanation.surface: An ancient athlete makes her debut in a Georgia city.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this huntress was a famously swift runner, beaten only by the golden apples trick.

clue.text: Prosecutor with bird's name?

parts.note: a crow is a black bird

explanation.surface: A question about a lawyer who goes by a bird's name.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain criminal cases are brought in the name of the Crown, so the Crown is the prosecutor.
explanation.definitionFit: In UK criminal law the state, styled the Crown, brings prosecutions, as in R v Smith.

clue.text: Sailors spend recklessly in the shade

parts.note: the navy is a body of sailors
to blue money is old British slang for squandering it

explanation.surface: Seamen on shore leave blow their pay in the shade.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a dark blue colour, the shade of naval uniforms.

clue.text: Appeal to teacher as to existence of deity?

parts.note: O is the vocative cry of appeal, as in O Lord
pupils address a male teacher as sir
is, as the verb of being, expresses existence

explanation.surface: A pupil asks the teacher whether God exists.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay reads as the pupil's question 'O sir, is (there a god)?'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the Egyptian god of the dead and the underworld.

clue.text: 8 was most of 11 a 3

parts.note: the two numbers that sum to eight, written as old money, were worth half (most of the letters of 11-across, halfway) of a crown (3-down)

explanation.surface: A puzzle of numbers referring to other answers in the grid.
explanation.walkthrough: 8 is not 8-down: it is the number eight, which two plus six makes. In pre-decimal British money two shillings and sixpence was half a crown; HALF is four of the seven letters of HALFWAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Two shillings and sixpence was the value of the half-crown coin in old British money.

clue.text: Don't drop the eggs!

definitions.meaning: to grip something tightly so it does not fall
a set of eggs laid at one time by a bird

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a warning to someone carrying eggs, but the two halves each define the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to grasp tightly and a batch of eggs laid together in a nest.

clue.text: Top church job, making tea — optional term

indicators.note: making means the following words are shaped into something new

explanation.surface: A senior church post seems to come with tea at a voluntary time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making' turns TEA, OPTIONAL and TERM, fifteen letters together, into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The office of a metropolitan, an archbishop over a province, is a top church post.

clue.text: Clubbers say "Perish the heretics!"

parts.note: to rot is to decay and perish
Arians followed the heresy of Arius, who denied Christ's full divinity

explanation.surface: Members of a club shout a curse at heretics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubbers' suggests nightclub-goers or people wielding clubs; it means members of a service club.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of Rotary International clubs are an example of people belonging to a club.

clue.text: See 23
Middle of the road prince with fairy around

parts.note: Prince Hal is Shakespeare's young Henry V

indicators.note: around means the fairy surrounds the next piece

parts.note: fay is an old word for fairy

explanation.surface: A centrist prince is accompanied by a fairy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something at the midpoint, or a moderate position, is in the middle of the road.

clue.text: He left heart (core) in confusion in place of fusion

indicators.note: in confusion means the remaining letters are jumbled
left means the letters of He have departed from the heart

explanation.surface: Someone abandons their heart to chaos in a fusion facility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' takes HE from HEART, leaving ART; 'in confusion' jumbles ART and CORE into the answer. 'fusion' echoing 'confusion' is a deliberate jingle.
explanation.definitionFit: A reactor is a plant where nuclear reactions, fission or fusion, take place.

clue.text: Bird of the wilderness

indicators.note: of means the bird is part of the word wilderness, a run within it

explanation.surface: A bird that lives in the wilds.
explanation.definitionFit: The erne is the sea eagle, a crossword favourite among birds.

clue.text: Contemporary village feature for union members only

definitions.meaning: a village store that has shut down, sadly common today
a workplace where only trade union members may be employed

explanation.surface: Modern villages are restricted to trade unionists.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is jokey: so many village shops have shut that one shut is now the typical sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a shop that has shut and a workplace requiring union membership share this phrase.

clue.text: Narrower at the bottom and the front, perhaps, and 17 25

definitions.text: Narrower at the bottom and the front, perhaps
definitions.meaning: a hull tapering to the keel and the bow, the outline of a vessel
the phrase at 17 and 25 across means neat and tidy, as on a well-run ship

explanation.surface: Describing a tapering form that is also orderly.
explanation.walkthrough: BRISTOL FASHION (17, 25) means in good order, a phrase from the port of Bristol.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as ship shape it describes a hull's form; as one word it means tidy and in good order.

clue.text: So I can do the weeding? That's novel

definitions.text: So I can do the weeding?
definitions.meaning: said by someone with a garden tool, 'I've an hoe', the answer run together

explanation.surface: A gardener says they can weed, and that's a book.
explanation.walkthrough: The first part is a pun: 'I've an hoe' (old-style 'an' before h) sounds like the title of Scott's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: This is Sir Walter Scott's 1819 historical romance of medieval England.

clue.text: This foal is born disorderly becoming orderly

indicators.note: disorderly means the fourteen letters are thrown out of order

explanation.surface: A newborn foal starts unruly but grows well-behaved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disorderly' jumbles THIS FOAL IS BORN; 'becoming' links. BRISTOL FASHION means in good order, from the busy port of Bristol.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'shipshape and Bristol fashion' means neat, tidy and in good order.

clue.text: Erif

parts.note: this is a word spelt backwards

explanation.walkthrough: ERIF is FIRE written back to front: the picture shows fire going back.
explanation.definitionFit: To go off wrongly or have the opposite effect to that intended is to rebound on its maker.

clue.text: Floss Miller gives fantastic traveller a new start

indicators.note: a new start means the first letter is swapped for another

parts.note: Gulliver is the traveller to fantastic lands in Swift's satire

explanation.surface: A mill owner gives a wandering figure a fresh beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Floss' refers to George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss; Mr Tulliver, Maggie's father, runs the mill. The new first letter T is not clued beyond 'a new start'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Tulliver is the miller of Dorlcote Mill in George Eliot's novel The Mill on the Floss.

clue.text: Studies a form of theft which gives …

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart
piracy is theft at sea or of copyright

explanation.surface: Learning about a kind of robbery leads on to the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs on into 22: a conspiracy gives a plot.
explanation.definitionFit: A conspiracy is a secret scheme, which produces a plot, the answer to the following clue.

clue.text: Rash Hotspur's danger?

definitions.meaning: a ... rash is an itchy skin eruption
Hotspur in Henry IV Part 1 says 'out of this ..., danger, we pluck this flower, safety'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rash' looks like an adjective describing the hot-headed Hotspur, but it is a skin rash.
explanation.definitionFit: A stinging plant whose sting brings up a rash, and Hotspur's emblem of danger.

clue.text: Confirm suitable retreat into light

indicators.note: into means the reversed piece goes inside the beam

parts.note: a ray is a beam of light

indicators.note: retreat means going back, so suitable is read backwards

parts.note: fit means suitable

explanation.surface: Approve a fitting withdrawal into the light.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retreat' looks like a noun after 'suitable', but it is the reversal signal working on the synonym for suitable.
explanation.definitionFit: To ratify a treaty or decision is to confirm it formally.

clue.text: … power to everyone with a piece of ground

parts.note: the lot means everyone, the whole lot

explanation.surface: Continuing the clue before, giving power to all with some land.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this to 19: the conspiracy gives a plot.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot is a small piece of land, as in a vegetable plot.

clue.text: Writer of Alice with words that are extraordinary

indicators.note: extraordinary means the letters are put into an unusual arrangement

explanation.surface: The author of Alice uses unusual vocabulary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer of Alice' points at Lewis Carroll, but 'of' and 'with' are links; ALICE and WORDS are jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde was an Irish playwright and novelist, author of The Importance of Being Earnest.

clue.text: Casual attempt at rhymes for 22

definitions.meaning: a random shot taken without careful aim
the two words of the answer each rhyme with the answer at 22-across, plot

explanation.surface: A careless try at finding rhymes.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is wordplay: both pot and shot rhyme with PLOT.
explanation.definitionFit: A pot shot is a careless or opportunistic attempt, originally shooting for the pot.

clue.text: See 17
Beginners for Pulitzer prize make a bloomer

indicators.note: make means those letters are made into a new word
beginners means the opening letters of Pulitzer prize are taken

explanation.surface: Novices who win a literary award make a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginners for' takes PULIT from the start of PULITZER, and 'make' jumbles it. 'bloomer' means a blunder on the surface, but here a flowering plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A tulip is a spring flower, something that blooms.

clue.text: Business agreement that's first and last made in heaven

parts.note: a firm is a business
amen is said in agreement
T is both the first and last letter of the word that

explanation.surface: A commercial deal is described as a match made in heaven.
explanation.definitionFit: The firmament is the vault of the sky, the heavens above.
